sections.title: An assignment acts on a state

passages.title: An assignment acts on a state
passages.text:
A state tells us the current value of each variable.

In a ← b, evaluate the right-hand side using the current state, then replace the value of a. The box called b keeps its value.

Equality a = b is instead a statement that two current values agree; it is not a command. The arrow points toward the destination.

A number copied now does not remain connected to its source.

sections.title: Why the obvious swap fails

passages.title: Why the obvious swap fails
passages.text:
To exchange two values, we want the final a to contain the original b and the final b to contain the original a.

Write those original values as a₀ and b₀. The commands a ← b; b ← a do not accomplish this: after the first command, a already contains b₀, so the second command copies b₀ again.

Both boxes finish with b₀. When a₀=b₀ the error is hidden by that particular input.

sections.title: Save, copy, restore

passages.title: Save, copy, restore
passages.text:
A temporary variable protects the value that would otherwise be overwritten.

Starting again from the same original state, execute t ← a, then a ← b, then b ← t. After the first command, t=a₀.

After the second, a=b₀ while t still equals a₀. The third command gives b=a₀.

Thus the postcondition is (a,b)=(b₀,a₀), including the case of equal original values. Resetting the demonstration is not a fourth operation in this three-assignment program.

sections.title: When one line captures both old values

passages.title: When one line captures both old values
passages.text:
Python evaluates the full right-hand side of a, b = b, a before assigning either target.

It therefore captures the old ordered pair (b₀,a₀), then assigns it to (a,b). This evaluation rule makes it a swap.

It is not the same execution as the two sequential commands a=b; b=a. A different language needs its own defined assignment semantics; mathematical equality alone supplies no execution order.

title: Build an induction proof

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition
source.note: Base case, inductive implication, and induction as a proof procedure; the triangular example is newly developed here. Original explanations, examples, and exercises; section references are a reading companion.

sections.title: A statement for every positive integer

passages.title: A statement for every positive integer
passages.text:
Let P(n) be the statement 1+2+⋯+n=n(n+1)/2 for positive integers n.

P(n) names a proposition, not a numerical sum. A drawing with four rows is one instance; the claim includes every allowed row count.

The first obligation is a direct proof of P(1): both sides equal 1. Without a true starting case, a chain of implications does not establish that any statement is true.

sections.title: Prove one reusable implication

passages.title: Prove one reusable implication
passages.text:
Fix an arbitrary positive integer k and assume P(k).

The assumption is used to prove an implication; we are not assuming the desired conclusion. The next sum consists of the old k rows plus a new row of k+1 cells.

Therefore its value is k(k+1)/2+(k+1)=(k+1)(k+2)/2, which is exactly the formula required by P(k+1). Since the algebra did not depend on a particular value of k, the implication applies at every step.

sections.title: Why the base and implication reach every case

passages.title: Why the base and implication reach every case
passages.text:
The base establishes P(1).

The proved implication then establishes P(2), then P(3), and so on. For any specified positive integer n, this proof construction reaches P(n) after finitely many applications.

There is no claim that we can animate infinitely many rows to finish the proof. The universal argument is that an arbitrary finite destination n can be reached using the same justified step.

Executable assertions check the displayed instances; they are not a substitute for the proof.

sections.title: A second view of the formula

passages.title: A second view of the formula
passages.text:
Take a second copy of the triangular array, rotate it, and place the copies together to fill an n by n+1 rectangle.

The rectangle contains n(n+1) cells, and each copy contains the same number, so one copy contains half that count. This is a general proof only when the arrangement is specified for arbitrary n; an attractive four-row picture alone proves only its own count.

The inductive argument has already supplied the required general justification.

sections.title: A pattern suggests a claim

passages.title: A pattern suggests a claim
passages.text:
For n=0,1,2,3, the polynomial f(n)=n²+n+11 gives 11,13,17,23, all prime.

A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose positive divisors are only 1 and itself. These observations support proposing a conjecture; they do not establish what happens at untested indices.

The domain matters: the proposed claim concerns every nonnegative integer, not merely four displayed inputs.

sections.title: One allowed failure defeats “every”

passages.title: One allowed failure defeats “every”
passages.text:
The universal conjecture is: for every n≥0, f(n) is prime.

To refute it, it is enough to exhibit one allowed n whose value is composite. A witness outside the domain would not refute the claim, and a different polynomial would not address it.

A finite computation can prove a claim over a specified finite domain by exhaustion; what it cannot do here is exhaust the infinite set of nonnegative integers.

sections.title: A concrete witness of compositeness

passages.title: A concrete witness of compositeness
passages.text:
At n=10, f(10)=100+10+11=121=11·11.

Both factors exceed 1, so this value is composite and the universal conjecture is false. The values for n=0 through 9 are prime, making the initial pattern persuasive but still inconclusive.

A factorization is a short witness: multiplication verifies it without searching every possible divisor.

sections.title: Proving one value prime is a different task

passages.title: Proving one value prime is a different task
passages.text:
To prove a particular positive integer x is prime, it is enough to rule out divisors 2 through floor(√x).

If x=uv with u,v>1, at least one of u,v is at most √x; otherwise their product would exceed x. Thus the finite search has a justified stopping bound.

This proves a statement about that one x. It does not prove that the polynomial produces primes at every index.

sections.title: The claim and its two starting cases

passages.title: The claim and its two starting cases
passages.text:
Define F₀=0, F₁=1 and F_k=F_{k−1}+F_{k−2} for k≥2.

We will prove the original teaching bound F_k≤2^(k−1) for every k≥1. The source uses a sharper bound involving φ; this simpler bound isolates the two-predecessor reasoning.

Check F₁=1≤1 and F₂=1≤2. Both are needed before a step that consults the preceding two cases.

Here 2^j denotes j factors of 2, with 2^0=1.

sections.title: Add the two earlier bounds

passages.title: Add the two earlier bounds
passages.text:
Fix k≥3 and assume the claim holds at every smaller positive index.

In particular, F_{k−1}≤2^(k−2) and F_{k−2}≤2^(k−3). Add these inequalities and use the recurrence: F_k≤2^(k−2)+2^(k−3)=3·2^(k−3)≤4·2^(k−3)=2^(k−1).

The last inequality is deliberately generous. We need a valid upper bound, not equality or the tightest bound.

Every hypothesis used has index smaller than k.

sections.title: Use earlier cases without circularity

passages.title: Use earlier cases without circularity
passages.text:
This argument uses the induction hypothesis for more than one earlier case.

It does not assume an unproved future value. Strong-induction wording permits all smaller positive indices as hypotheses, though this proof needs only the two immediate predecessors.

Ordinary and strong induction can prove the same class of statements; the latter is a convenient organization. The special start at k=3 prevents an illicit use of a bound at index zero, where our stated claim does not begin.

sections.title: An assertion belongs to a place

passages.title: An assertion belongs to a place
passages.text:
Use the array a=[2,5,1,4].

At the loop test, maintain 0≤k≤length and the assertion that s is the sum of the first k entries. The first k entries have indices 0 through k−1.

Initially k=0,s=0, so the processed prefix is empty and the assertion holds. This is a statement about a particular program location, not a promise about every instant of execution.

At the final test, k<length is false.

sections.title: Why the loop also finishes

passages.title: Why the loop also finishes
passages.text:
Correctness of the exit value does not by itself show that the exit is reached.

Here length−k is a nonnegative integer at every loop test, and each completed body decreases it by one. A strictly decreasing sequence of nonnegative integers cannot continue forever.

Thus the loop terminates. For an empty array, initialization already gives k=length=0 and s=0; the test fails immediately, with no array access.

sections.title: A signed recipe using fixed originals

passages.title: A signed recipe using fixed originals
passages.text:
For fixed positive integers m and n, seek integers a,b such that am+bn=d, where d=gcd(m,n).

The coefficients may be negative: a negative multiple is subtracted. In this lesson m=26,n=15 remain the original inputs throughout.

The changing Euclidean remainders have separate names. We first find d by ordinary Euclid, then retrace the equations to construct a recipe using only the originals.

sections.title: Store equations rather than only results

passages.title: Store equations rather than only results
passages.text:
Euclid gives 26=1·15+11, 15=1·11+4, 11=2·4+3, 4=1·3+1, and 3=3·1+0.

Therefore the last nonzero remainder is 1. Each nonzero remainder can be rewritten as dividend minus quotient times divisor.

Keeping these equations preserves the information needed for back-substitution; the bare list of remainder values would not record which earlier values created each one.

sections.title: Replace a remainder by its stored recipe

passages.title: Replace a remainder by its stored recipe
passages.text:
Start from 1=4−3.

Replace 3 by 11−2·4 to get 1=3·4−11. Replace 4 by 15−11 to get 1=3·15−4·11.

Finally replace 11 by 26−15 to get 1=−4·26+7·15. Each replacement substitutes equal expressions, and each coefficient must distribute over the entire replacement.

After combining like terms, only the original inputs remain. The value stays 1 throughout, although the expression changes.

sections.title: Check the result and its scope

passages.title: Check the result and its scope
passages.text:
The constructed coefficients are a=−4,b=7: −4·26+7·15=−104+105=1.

Euclid already established gcd(26,15)=1, so this is the requested identity. The coefficients are not necessarily unique.

Every common divisor of 26 and 15 divides any integer combination of them; in particular it divides 1, another way to verify that these inputs are coprime. For a general identity am+bn=d, also establishing that d is a positive common divisor would prove d is the gcd.

An unexplained identity alone is not sufficient.

title: Carry coefficients forward

source.book: Donald E. Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 1, third edition
source.note: Extended Euclid and its two linear-combination invariants. Original explanations, examples, and exercises; section references are a reading companion.

sections.title: Attach a recipe to each working length

passages.title: Attach a recipe to each working length
passages.text:
Keep m=26,n=15 fixed.

The changing Euclidean pair is c,d. Alongside it, maintain c=a′m+b′n and d=am+bn whenever control reaches the division step.

Initially c=m,d=n, so take a′=1,b′=0,a=0,b=1. The prime is a label for the first coefficient row, not a derivative.

Two rows are necessary because the next remainder subtracts a multiple of d from c.

sections.title: Subtract recipes with the same quotient

passages.title: Subtract recipes with the same quotient
passages.text:
At division, c=qd+r.

Substitute the two maintained identities: r=(a′m+b′n)−q(am+bn)=(a′−qa)m+(b′−qb)n. Thus the new coefficient pair is u=a′−qa,v=b′−qb.

Compute both using the old rows before overwriting either. In the first pass, 26=1·15+11 and the new recipe is 11=1·26−1·15.

This algebra proves preservation; the displayed arithmetic illustrates it.

sections.title: Move recipes with their lengths

passages.title: Move recipes with their lengths
passages.text:
After computing the remainder and its coefficients, promote the old d row to the c row and place the remainder row into the d row.

This is a movement of complete packages: a length must not become separated from the coefficient pair that reconstructs it. A sequential implementation needs temporary storage; a simultaneous assignment is safe only if all right-hand values are captured first.

At the next division both identities hold again.

sections.title: Read the gcd and its certificate

passages.title: Read the gcd and its certificate
passages.text:
When the remainder is zero, the current divisor d is the gcd of the original inputs because ordinary Euclid has preserved their common divisors.

The second-row invariant simultaneously gives am+bn=d. Here the result is d=1,a=−4,b=7.

The algorithm returns a value and an exact recipe for it. Termination follows from strict descent of the positive working divisor d on continuing passes, not from the behavior of the signed coefficients, which may grow in magnitude.
